$comment: ENTIRELY FICTIONAL. Meridian Bank does not exist. Every value below is an invented placeholder created to exercise the prototype — none of it is a real bank policy, a real cost, or a verified fact about IndusInd Bank, Yes Bank or any other issuer. A deliberately fictional name is used so this can never be mistaken for real issuer data. The only fields traceable to the real application are marked with sourcedFrom.

bank.note: Invented for prototype testing. Not a real institution.

channels.$comment: Channel names and the delivery-status vocabulary are real (from the app). Costs, caps and availability below are INVENTED. relativeCost is an ordinal placeholder, not a currency amount, precisely so it cannot be misread as a real rate card.
channels.sourcedFrom: channel names: src/data/sharedConstants.ts CHANNEL_CONFIG_LABELS (real). All cost/limit values: invented.

available.note: modelled as unavailable to exercise the agent's constraint handling

hardConstraints.$comment: INVENTED. Modelled as hard so the prototype can exercise 'constraint must win over preference'. A real deployment would source these from the issuer and have them approved. A per-campaign message cap was removed: it is not an issuer policy. How many messages a campaign sends is a design decision that differs per campaign — a two-week nurture and a three-day expiry reminder are not the same number — and carrying one here made the agent budget against it ('two sends against a permitted four') instead of designing for the goal.

quietHours.$comment: INVENTED window, retained ONLY to exercise the prototype. Not a verified issuer policy. Quiet hours are issuer-level configuration owned by the Drip Campaign system; the agent reads a window it is given and must never define one. A real deployment must source this from that system, not from here.
quietHours.enforcedBy: Drip Campaign runtime at send time. The agent only validates the campaign's configured send times at design time.
quietHours.sourceNote: Quiet hours exist as a real implemented guardrail in the nudges platform's Frequency Limits step (see principles P-004). These from/to VALUES are invented.

minHoursBetweenMessages.$comment: A PREFERENCE against nagging, not a hard constraint. The key and its value are kept so planner.ts still reads them. Same day is fine when they have just opened or clicked, and the night window from quietHours 21:00-09:00 still applies. Do not space every message 48 hours apart as a rule.

softPreferences.$comment: INVENTED. Preferences, not constraints — the agent may trade these off and must say when it does.

preferLowerCostChannelFirst.$comment: Do not lead with email because it is cheap. WhatsApp and in-app are how people actually read in this market, and cost per message is not reach. When this is false the build orders fallback channels WhatsApp, SMS, email, RCS rather than by price.

notes: No appetite is on file for this issuer, so design the full plan.
Do not thin the messages or drop tests to be safe. An unstated appetite is missing information, not a request for restraint.
If the manager states an appetite later, trim then and say what you removed.

eventsCalendar.$comment: INVENTED dates for a fictional bank. Not a real festive/promotional calendar.

makerChecker.$comment: The MECHANISM is real — computeMakerCheckerFlag() in the app decides this from issuer and program flags. The value below is an invented stand-in for the fictional bank.

knownGaps: No real channel costs — relativeCost is ordinal and invented.
No campaign performance history for this bank (none exists anywhere in the prototype).
The app itself holds no cost, quiet-hours or frequency-cap fields at all — verified by grep. Nothing here is enforced by the application today.

market.$comment: REAL, unlike the rest of this file. The BANK here is fictional; the MARKET is not. These are facts about the Indian credit-card market that the agent was previously designing without — it had no idea which country, currency, regulator or messaging regime it was writing for. Each item carries its own confidence: 'established' is something the agent may rely on, 'verify-with-compliance' is directionally right and must not be stated to a campaign manager as settled.
market.whoTheCustomersAre: Retail credit-card holders of Indian banks. The campaign manager works at the issuer.

currency.note: Write amounts as ₹ with Indian digit grouping (₹1,20,000 not ₹120,000). Large sums are spoken in lakh (1,00,000) and crore (1,00,00,000); a manager will say 'two lakh', not '200 thousand'.

regulator.name: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
regulator.note: Named so the agent knows which regime it is in. WHAT THE RULES REQUIRE DOES NOT COME FROM HERE. Specific obligations — activation windows, consent mechanics, registered message templates, retention, grievance timelines — are issuer-specific compliance context that the bank supplies in its own hardConstraints. Never infer a rule, never cite one, and never tell a campaign manager what the regulator requires. If a design depends on a compliance question, raise it as an open item for their compliance team and carry on.

channelReality.note: WhatsApp is a primary channel for Indian retail banking customers and is often read where email is not. In-app is primary too: a cardholder who has the issuer's app open is already in a position to act. Email open rates are typically far weaker than in Western markets, so do not treat email as the default first touch just because it costs least per message. PLAN WITH IN-APP WHERE IT FITS. The builder cannot send in-app yet, so after the plan is approved, map those steps to WhatsApp or SMS and say in the plan that you have done so. Never propose a send on a channel the issuer does not have.

competingForSpend.note: UPI dominates everyday low-value payments in India. A new credit card is therefore not competing only with other cards but with a free, instant, habitual rail. 'Why use the card at all' is a real customer question, which matters for activation and first-spend campaigns.

emiIsMainstream.note: Converting a purchase or an outstanding balance to EMI is an everyday, heavily marketed product in India, and 'no-cost EMI' is a familiar construct to customers. An EMI campaign is not introducing a novel idea; it is competing for attention against the merchant's own EMI offer at checkout.

seasonality.note: The festive quarter around Diwali (roughly October to November) is the peak of discretionary card spend, and merchant discounting is heaviest then. Timing a campaign into or away from it is a real strategic choice, not a detail.

language.note: English is normal for urban cardholders, but plain English beats formal English, and a mix of English with local-language words is common in real usage. Write short sentences. Avoid idiom that does not travel.
